system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman was admitted with right lower quadrant pain, fever, and nausea two weeks after laparoscopic appendectomy. CT imaging revealed a periappendiceal abscess, which was successfully drained percutaneously under CT guidance. She was managed with IV fluids, pain control, and transitioned to oral antibiotics (ciprofloxacin and metronidazole). Her symptoms improved, and she was discharged home after three days with instructions to complete a 10-day antibiotic course and follow up in two weeks for repeat imaging. Her psychiatric and chronic medical conditions were maintained on home medications without complication.
problems: Major depressive affective disorder, single episode, unspecified

radiology_notes.text:
CLINICAL INDICATION:  Left lower quadrant intermittent pain.  Evaluate for
torsion.

TECHNIQUE:  Grayscale, color and spectral Doppler ultrasound evaluation of the
pelvis via a transabdominal approach and subsequently via a transvaginal
approach for better delineation of anatomy.

COMPARISON:  Pelvic ultrasound ___.

FINDINGS:  The uterus measures 6.1 x 2.2 x 3.7 cm.  The endometrium is
homogeneous.  The right ovary contains a 2-cm simple cyst.  Both ovaries
appear normal and demonstrate normal arterial and venous waveforms.  No free
fluid is identified.

IMPRESSION:  Normal-appearing uterus and ovaries.  Arterial and venous
waveforms demonstrated in both ovaries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. ___ from the gynecology team. I understand you've been having pelvic pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s this sharp pain on the left side, near my lower belly. It comes and goes, lasts about 20 seconds, and shoots down to my rectum and leg. It’s been going on for three days now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And does this feel like your usual endometriosis flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s pretty similar. I tried naproxen and a heating pad, but nothing helped much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. We’ve checked your vitals and blood work. Your white count is normal, and your pregnancy test came back negative, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there an infection then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we don’t think so. Your labs don’t show signs of infection. We also did an ultrasound to check your ovaries and uterus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. What did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — everything looks normal. The uterus and ovaries appear fine, no cysts or signs of torsion. No free fluid either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So if everything’s normal, why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely an acute flare of your endometriosis. Sometimes the pain can be severe even when imaging doesn’t show active changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. What will help it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with stronger pain meds — Dilaudid for now, and we’ll add gabapentin, ibuprofen, and Tylenol to help control the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today? You seemed more comfortable overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better, actually. Still there, but not as intense. I was able to sleep a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Since you’re stable and improving, we’re planning to discharge you today with oral medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What should I take at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue gabapentin three times a day, ibuprofen every six hours as needed, and tramadol or Tylenol for breakthrough pain. And remember to take ibuprofen with food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Should I be worried if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop a fever, severe pain, heavy bleeding, or can’t keep fluids down, call your doctor or come back. Otherwise, follow up with Dr. ___ in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I feel better knowing it’s not something more serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready, and the nurse will go over the meds again before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before discharge. Any new symptoms or concerns?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, still feeling about the same — manageable pain. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember to take your lithium as usual, and keep up with your asthma and reflux meds too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have all my regular meds at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re cleared to go home. Take care, and follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate your help.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman with a history of endometriosis was admitted for acute-on-chronic left lower quadrant pelvic pain radiating to the rectum and leg. Initial evaluation revealed stable vital signs after pain control, normal white blood cell count, negative pregnancy test, and a normal pelvic ultrasound with no evidence of torsion or free fluid. Pain was managed with intravenous and oral analgesics, including Dilaudid, tramadol, gabapentin, ibuprofen, and acetaminophen. Given the absence of infectious or structural causes, the pain was attributed to an endometriosis flare. She improved clinically and was discharged home on hospital day two with a regimen of oral pain medications and follow-up instructions.
